newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH - Government finances still heading south.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - Government finances still heading south.

text.p: Canberra's finances worsened again in August, five months after the new government took power and began to tighten spending.

This is evident from a rolling, 12-month analysis of last week's Commonwealth Government Statement of Financial Transactions (commonly abbreviated as CFT, from an earlier and shorter version of the name).
The latest 12-month underlying balance is A$13.1 billion, up from A$12.6 billion the previous month.
Running one's eye along the results for the past year, it is difficult to discern any trend improvement. The conclusion -- government finances are wallowing.
The latest data also backs up the suspicion that June's 12-month number of A$10.3 billion, which goes into the history books as the 1995/96 result, was a flash in the pan.
The June result just happened to be the best in years and was sandwiched between substantially worse data in other months.
In issuing last week's data, Finance Minister John Fahey said revenue for July and August was down 9.6 percent on the same period a year before.
The key declines, he said, were in tax collections from companies and superannuation funds, both of which had been affected by a changed in the payment pattern.
That factor may adequately explain the budget's weakness.
So far this fiscal year, the government is down about A$3.5 billion on tax from companies and superannuation funds compared with the previous year.
By contrast, the government is banking on eight percent company tax growth for the full year.

If one assumes that that cash will eventually flow into the Treasury, it becomes easier to see the government closing the huge gap between the latest A$13.1 billion underlying 12-month deficit and the A$5.6 billion it has forecast for June 1997.
